newsitem.title: JAPAN: G7 meet won't stem Japan capital outflow - dealers.
newsitem.headline: G7 meet won't stem Japan capital outflow - dealers.

text.p: This weekend's meeting of the Group of Seven (G7) nations is unlikely to stop Japanese capital flowing overseas, dealers said on Friday.
"The ongoing capital flow out of Japan can't be stopped whatever of the results of the G7 meeting," said Noriyuki Mizukami, head of Treasury sales at National Westminster Bank in Tokyo.
Finance ministers and central bank governors of the G7 -- the United States, Japan, Germany, France, Britain, Italy and Canada -- meet in Berlin on Saturday.

The other six nations are seen supporting a call by Japan to stabilise currency rates, but the impact may fizzle out because doubts remain over whether they will join hands to prop up the sagging yen, dealers said.
On Friday, the dollar rose as high as 124.30 yen in afternoon Tokyo, posting a fresh 48-month high.

Currency dealers said the root of the yen's recent fall to more than 120 yen to the dollar lay in Japan itself and that months of rock-bottom interest rates had swollen the outflow of Japanese capital.
"Those who particularly boosted their dollar purchases after 120 yen were not foreign hedge funds but a wide range of Japanese investors," said a senior trader at a Japan bank.

Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, speaking to reporters ahead of his departure for Berlin, reiterated Japan's view that both an excessive weakness or strength in the yen is unfavourable, and said this would be Tokyo's stance at the G7.
Mitsuzuka said all G7 nations agree that stable foreign exchange markets are important for each economy, but did not say whether he would ask them for any concerted action.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said in a newspaper interview on Friday that there was no sense in trying to set exchange rate targets at this weekend's G7 meeting.
Asked whether the group would accede to Japan's wish for exchange-rate goals, Waigel told Die Welt that exchange rates could not be determined with statements.
"It is not possible to determine exchange rates, but you can adopt the required policy and then implement it. Every country must do its homework. That applies to Japan."
The German mark also sunk to a 32-month low against dollar on Friday, hitting 1.6599 in late Tokyo.
"Under the circumstances, it would be difficult for Japan to take the lead in drawing up a specific accord to check the yen's excessive falls," the senior trader said.

The rush to jump on foreign-currency investments, which promise far higher returns as long as exchange rates are stable, seem to have attracted public entities as well as the private sector, dealers said.
They said that on Thursday, a major Japanese public fund actively bought large amounts of U.S. government notes and dollars.
The government arm continued to buy even after the greenback rose above 120 yen, and was said to be one of driving forces behind the dollar's rise to a four-year high of 124 yen.

Overseas funds had played a key role in pushing the dollar up to 120 yen after its plunge to a post-war record low of 79.55 yen in April 1995, but dealers said foreign operators now seemed somewhat at a loss over the speed of the dollar's rise.
Although an increase in domestic interest rates by the Bank of Japan (BOJ) would effectively stem the dollar's rise as well as capital outflow from Japan, dealers said this was unlikely.
Renewed worries about the health of Japanese financial institutions related to their huge bad loans would make it difficult for Tokyo to take that step for now.
